title: Given balloons with values, bursting balloon i yields nums[left]·nums[i]·nums[right] where left and right are the adjacent unburst balloons. Maximize the total coins from bursting all balloons.
shortTitle: Burst Balloons — interval DP choosing the last balloon to burst

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP over an array padded with 1 at both ends. dp[i][j] is the max coins from bursting all balloons strictly between i and j. Choose k as the LAST balloon burst in (i,j): dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i]·nums[k]·nums[j] + dp[k][j]. Time O(n³), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A liquidation desk at National Bank of India closes positions one by one, where each closure's payout depends on its two surviving neighbors. The trick is to decide which position is closed LAST in a range, because then its neighbors are the fixed boundaries, splitting the range cleanly into two independent subranges.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick the LAST balloon to burst in the interval; its neighbors are the padded boundaries.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP over an array padded with 1 at both ends. dp[i][j] is the max coins from bursting all balloons strictly between i and j. Choose k as the LAST balloon burst in (i,j): dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i]·nums[k]·nums[j] + dp[k][j]. Time O(n³), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A liquidation desk at National Bank of India closes positions one by one, where each closure's payout depends on its two surviving neighbors. The trick is to decide which position is closed LAST in a range, because then its neighbors are the fixed boundaries, splitting the range cleanly into two independent subranges.

**One line to remember:** Pick the LAST balloon to burst in the interval; its neighbors are the padded boundaries.

sections.s2_technical:
The difficulty is that bursting a balloon changes who its neighbors are, so thinking about the FIRST balloon to burst couples the two sides. The insight is to instead pick the LAST balloon k to burst in an open interval (i, j). When k is last, every other balloon in the interval is already gone, so k's neighbors are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j, which decouples the left and right subranges.

Pad the array with a one at each end so boundary multiplications are well defined. Then dp[i][j] over the open interval is the maximum over all k strictly between i and j of dp[i][k] plus nums[i] times nums[k] times nums[j] plus dp[k][j]. For example: `dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[k][j]);`. Iterate by increasing interval length so subintervals are ready. The answer is dp[0][n+1] over the padded array.

The time is O(n³) from three nested loops and space is O(n²). A senior nuance is that this "choose the last operation" reframing is the signature trick of hard interval DPs, the same idea powering matrix-chain multiplication.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a liquidation desk closes positions one at a time, and each closure's payout depends on the two still-open neighboring positions, so the order of closures changes total proceeds. This is exactly how Burst Balloons works.

Problem 2 — Reasoning about which position closes first couples both sides, but reasoning about which closes last fixes the boundaries. This is exactly why the DP chooses the last balloon in each interval.

The mini-project builds a `LiquidationOptimizer`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input values are three, one, five, eight.

Step 1: The array is padded to one, three, one, five, eight, one so boundary multiplications are defined.

Step 2: Short intervals are solved first, computing the best coins for single-balloon ranges.

Step 3: For each larger interval the code tries every balloon as the last one burst, using the padded boundaries as the surviving neighbors.

Step 4: The subrange results combine, and the best choice of last balloon is kept for each interval.

Step 5: The full interval yields one hundred sixty-seven, and the two-element case yields ten.

```text
    dp[i][j] = max over k   (k = LAST balloon burst)
  answer = dp[0][n+1] = 167
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Burst Balloons is a hard interval dynamic programming problem, and the whole difficulty is that bursting a balloon changes who its neighbors are. If I reason about which balloon to burst first, the two sides stay coupled because the first burst's neighbors keep shifting. The key insight is to flip the reasoning and pick which balloon is burst last within an interval.

When a balloon k is the last to burst in an open interval between i and j, every other balloon in that interval is already gone, so k's neighbors are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j. That decouples the interval into an independent left part and right part. I pad the array with a one at each end so the boundary multiplications are defined, and then dp of i and j is the maximum over every choice of last balloon k of the left subinterval, plus the product of the two boundaries with k, plus the right subinterval. I fill intervals by increasing length, and the answer spans the whole padded array.

In my project at National Bank of India, a liquidation desk closed positions one at a time where each closure's payout depended on the two still-open neighbors, so the order changed the total proceeds. I used this choose-the-last-operation reframing, which is the same signature trick behind matrix-chain multiplication, and it runs in cubic time.
